title: Tisha B'Av, lived
hookLine: sitting low, reading Lamentations, remembering sorrows old and new
tomorrow: after the floor, what does the prophet say first?

lines: ON THE FLOOR, IN DIM LIGHT.
cards: Chairs are how we tell the world we're fine. On one day a year, in synagogues, people get off them.
They sit on the floor or on low stools, in dim light, some without leather shoes, and they listen to a book chanted in a slow, falling tune. Why do people sit on the floor one day a year?
Because that's where mourners sit. Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, is a day of mourning for the Temple in Jerusalem, and for sorrows that came after.

teach.b: The book is Lamentations, in Hebrew Eichah, named for its first word: how. "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" A city sitting alone, like a widow.
The reader's voice drops into its mournful tune, and the room goes quiet enough to hear pages turn.
Tradition says other sorrows fell on this date too, and communities add kinot, elegies, for griefs across the centuries, old and new.
Then the body joins in. Low seats. No eating or drinking, for those who fast.
Some don't greet each other with hello. The point isn't drama. It's letting the body say what words can't: something was lost, and it hasn't been forgotten.
Here's a detail to tell a friend. Lamentations doesn't end on hope; its last verse is bleak.
So when it's read aloud, the verse before it is said again, and the book closes on a plea: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old."
Even on the floor, the tradition won't let despair have the last word.
Around midday, people rise from the floor. The grief isn't over. It just has a shape, and a time to stand.

how: On Tisha B'Av, Jews who keep it fast from sunset to nightfall, sit on the floor or low seats until about midday, hear Lamentations chanted in synagogue, and recite kinot, elegies for the Temple and later sorrows.

o: the fast that closes the Days of Awe in the fall
a happy feast for the giving of the Torah
the ninth of Av, a day of mourning for the Temple

games.q: a day kept low — tap the pairs.
p: elegies for old and new sorrows
so the book ends on a plea

s: Lamentations ends on a hopeful verse
its last verse is bleak; the verse before is said again so the reading closes on a plea.
on Tisha B'Av people sit on the floor or low seats until around midday
the way mourners sit. then they rise.
Tisha B'Av only remembers one event long ago
it mourns the Temple and, with added kinot, sorrows old and new.

games.q: Tisha B'Av, around noon. your aunt gets up off the floor and sits in a chair. your cousin says she's quitting early. what's happening?
o: the custom: low seats until around midday, then people rise.
she's breaking the fast, which always ends at noon.
she's finished mourning; the whole day ends at noon.
games.why: around midday mourners rise from the floor, while those who fast keep fasting until night. the grief has a shape, and a time to stand.

practice: If you can, move from your chair to the floor, or to the lowest seat nearby. Let your shoulders drop and rest your hands open in your lap.
For the length of the sit, stay low, and let one sorrow, old or new, yours or the world's, sit there with you, without trying to fix it.

wordCard.voice: Tisha B'Av: the ninth of Av, a day of mourning for the Temple and the sorrows since, kept low, on the floor, with Lamentations.

orig.note: Hebrew: how; the first word, and the Hebrew name, of Lamentations.

carryVoice: Keep this close: sit low, and let grief have its shape, and its time to stand. See you tomorrow.
